chapter_theme: In the forest a married woman who has hidden from her husband begs Civakan to take her, and he answers by stripping the body to its humours, tissues and worms and blaming the kavya poets for painting it; her husband Pavadattan arrives lamenting her loss to a yakshi, Civakan consoles him with praise of learning and a two-sided teaching on women's frailty and the rare chaste wife, laughs at his faith in her, and with a mantra sends him to find her, after which Civakan climbs a holy hill thronged by pilgrims shedding their sins.

cast.role: the hero, travelling alone through the forest; called முழவுத் தோளான் and இளையான் here
the woman who approaches Civakan in the grove, claiming at 1580 to have been dropped by a Vidyadhara; Pavadattan's wife (not named in these verses)
a learned man of the middle country, husband of the woman, searching for her in the forest
the yakshi Pavadattan believes has carried off his wife
the women climbing the holy hill to be rid of their sins
the crowds of worshippers carrying offerings up the hill

1581.reading: The woman pleads that she suffers like a motherless child, that seeing him, the cherished husband of women with bamboo-like shoulders, she has reached heaven, and that if he leaves her without grace she will destroy her life, as if nectar were poured into fire.
1581.event: The woman in the grove begs Civakan to take her and threatens to die if he refuses.
1581.nuance: She has just told him (1580) that she is a woman dropped in the forest by a Vidyadhara; the husband's lament that follows shows she is a married woman who has hidden from her husband, so the plea is an attempt on another man's wife's part to seduce the hero.

1582.reading: Civakan answers the girl sick with desire, who has fainted thinking of his shoulders like bars of gems, his chest broad as a hill, his lotus eyes and his sun-like face: listen to this.
1582.event: Civakan turns to answer the woman's advance.
1582.nuance: He first recites her praise of his own body, so that the lecture that follows takes apart the very features she desires, starting with his and moving to hers.

1583.reading: He says that the hair which is bathed in flowers and musk, wreathed in fragrant smoke and where jasmine garlands sleep is in truth wind, bile and phlegm, harmful filth, blood, flesh, bone, fat, marrow, entrails, mean skin, sinews and grease.

claims.claim: the adorned body is only humours and foul matter beneath its scents and flowers

1583.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are the love poet's adorned hair; lines 3 and 4 strip it in one breath into the three humours and the body's tissues, so that the sentence turns at குரைவளி பித்தோ டையே.

1584.reading: He says it is a worm-filled hut of fat, white poison, nails, hair and the rheum the eyes spit out; when the miserable flesh is cut and split open, who could bear to look, with crows pecking at the eyes, though by its nature it appears like gold, O creeper.

claims.claim: the body is a worm-infested hut that only appears golden

1584.nuance: Line 2 (தடிதடித் கீழ்ந்த) and line 3 (பிள்ளையார் கண்ணுட் காக்கை) are hard to construe; the general sense, the opened body as carrion, is clear, but the precise picture is not.

1585.reading: He says that if she calls it beauty, it is a full bag of skin on which brows, eyes and nose have been painted to be seen: is there anything in it worth a thought? The poets of kavya have dressed up this mass of flesh so that the fire of desire may rise.

claims.claim: beauty is paint on a skin bag, and poets elaborate the flesh in order to kindle desire

1585.nuance: காப்பியக் கவிகள் names the kind of poem the Cintamani itself is: the hero condemns the genre that has just spent many verses (1482-1484 and the descriptions of this grove) doing what he describes.

1586.reading: The husband, searching, cries to the young daughter of his loving uncle that he would praise her nature, saying that her waist would break even if a bee sat on her dark hair; while he wastes in pain like the surging sea, is it a virtue in her, the creeper, to hide herself away?
1586.event: A man searching the grove laments to his vanished wife, his uncle's daughter.
1586.nuance: The metre changes here and the voice is new: the man is named only at 1594. Line 4 (பேறால்வா யொளித்தொழிதல்) says she hid herself; he takes her vanishing as a game or a cruelty, not yet as a theft.

1587.reading: He asks whether her moon face holds swords or dark carp, a devouring Death, a bright spear or flowers, he cannot tell, and calls her sweet-voiced, doll with firm breasts, creeper, honey, nectar, his own life: where has she gone?
1587.nuance: The stock similes for eyes that Civakan has just called the poets' paint return at once in the husband's mouth, unanswered.

1588.reading: He says that her small feet, fair as silk-cotton buds, falter in fear, so that when she walks the golden anklets the craftsman made laugh at the flowers on the ground, and she steps aside onto flowers; peacock-like woman, he cannot give up the love in his eyes.
1588.nuance: Line 3 seems to say she treads on his life as on flowers (என்னாவி மலர்மேன் மிதித்து), a lover's conceit; the construction is loose.

1589.reading: He recalls that he saw her playing ball among her attendants and swooned, and while he lay lovesick she, hearing of it from others, sent word to be resolved and come; he came, and now, while he suffers, she of the jewelled girdle gives no answer and hides.
1589.event: The husband recalls how their love began and complains that she will not answer.
1589.nuance: The courtship he recalls was her choice as much as his (she sent the word துணிக போதும்), which sharpens the irony of her present flight.

1590.reading: Addressing a yakshi, he says she must have bewitched his wife and carried her off to destroy her beauty, thinking it equal to her own, and begs her to give back his lady, promising all she desires; worshipping, he grows bewildered like a good elephant that has lost its strong mate.
1590.event: The husband prays to a yakshi he believes has stolen his wife.
1590.nuance: Line 4 shifts to the narrator's simile. Civakan had wondered at 1570 whether the woman herself was a yakshi (இயக்கிகொல்); now the husband blames a yakshi for taking her, and Civakan will use the same belief at 1600.

1591.reading: He says that he has brought grief to famous Thathan of the fertile middle country's great town where bees embrace the lotus, to his dear Sinadattai, to Selvanaman, to Chittiramamalai and to all their kin: if he goes back, what will he say, what will he do?
1591.nuance: The kin are named but their relation to him and to her (whose parents are which) is not stated in the verse and the division of the names (செல்வநா மற்கு) is uncertain.

1592.reading: He says she told him she was faint with thirst, so he searched the forest, came upon a pond and brought water folded in a fine lotus leaf; and the noble man, unable to bear it, weeps and weeps, burns, melts and wastes.
1592.event: The husband tells that his wife sent him for water and was gone when he returned.
1592.nuance: This is the first plain account of how she came to be alone, and it contradicts the story she told Civakan at 1580 of being carried off by a Vidyadhara and dropped in the forest.

1593.reading: Not finding his bangled wife, the handsome man wept and spoke; the young man with drum-like shoulders, having seen and heard the jewel-garlanded woman's desire, smiled, said softly 'stay here', and went to the young man.
1593.event: Civakan smiles, bids someone stay where they are, and goes to the weeping husband.
1593.nuance: Whom Civakan tells to stay (இருநீ) is not said; the sense that fits is the hidden woman. His smile marks that he alone knows both sides of the story.

1594.reading: When Civakan asks what has befallen him and what his name is, he says: hero of shoulders shining like a golden hill, by my sin I have lost here a woman like a golden flowering creeper; I am Pavadattan, learned in many treatises.
1594.event: Civakan asks the man his trouble and name, and he gives his name as Pavadattan and tells of his loss.

claims.claim: one's loss comes from one's own sin

1594.nuance: He ascribes the loss to his own பாவம, though the story has shown it is his wife's doing; and he names his learning as his identity, which Civakan takes up at once.

1595.reading: Civakan says that learning, bought even by giving away one's wealth, becomes an eye once learned, a companion to the heart in its weakness, yielding the true thing; all else is false, while learning is gold, fame and a wife to a man: having this, why do you grieve?

claims.claim: learning is true wealth and a support in grief, all other things being false

1595.nuance: துணைவி யாக்கும் is pointed: learning itself is offered as a wife to a man who has lost his wife.

1596.reading: He says that though love's garland, strung with affection for thread, sweet words for flowers, and dipped in the sandal of desire, is worn in full day and never comes apart, for young women a heart that follows others is not hard.

claims.claim: however well a man's love binds a woman, her heart can still follow another

1596.nuance: Line 4 (பின்செலும் பிறார்க ணுள்ளம் பிணையனார்க் கடியதன்றே) is read as 'for doe-like women it is not hard for the heart to go after others'; the word பிறார்கண் looks miswritten.

1597.reading: He says: listen to what women are: they have no dignity, they do not regard birth, they do not hold their restraint within, they have a thousand minds; if a man counts to ten and presses, even Indra's daughter melts there like a hill of butter in fire and follows.

claims.claim: women lack inner restraint and yield to persistent pressing

1597.nuance: The speech is aimed at a man who has just praised his wife as true, and the hero knows that this wife has just tried to seduce him; the epic gives its general claim about women an occasion that seems to confirm it, then qualifies it in the next verse.

1598.reading: He goes on that there are also women who die if he dies; when the husband is away they wear no flowers and live forlorn in their dignity, never speak of Kama, live worshipping their husband's hands, are like Tiru of the honeyed flower, and end the distress of the man they have joined.

claims.claim: a chaste wife dies with her husband, renounces adornment in his absence and lives worshipping him

1598.nuance: Read against 1597 this is the exception that keeps the rule: chastity is described by the absence of desire (காமனை யென்றுஞ் சொல்லார்) and by the husband's absence, which is precisely the condition Pavadattan's wife has just failed.

1599.reading: Pavadattan says, sir, his companion is like that: having seen him with her eyes she never afterwards looked at another, a woman of great innocence; how can he live having lost her? To him who grieved so, the man of jewelled drum-like shoulders laughed: 'is she so?'
1599.event: Pavadattan insists his wife is of the chaste kind, and Civakan laughs.
1599.nuance: The husband's claim is exactly what the reader has seen to be false (1581); Civakan's laugh is the only comment the hero makes, and he does not expose her.

1600.reading: Civakan tells him not to grieve: recite this mantra and go the length of one bowshot, and the yakshi will bring her and give her to you, and you will have your bangled woman; he goes, sees the woman there, embraces her feet, falls and cries out.
1600.event: Civakan gives Pavadattan a mantra and sends him a bowshot away, where he finds his wife and falls at her feet.
1600.nuance: The yakshi is the husband's own story; Civakan uses it rather than telling the truth, so that the wife is returned without shame and the husband's belief in her is kept.

1601.reading: He told her all he had suffered without holding back, and she heard; she let go her desire for the other man and turned her love to this one, and her husband, clinging to the garlanded woman with a longing that would not part, praised her beauty.
1601.event: Pavadattan tells his wife his grief; she gives up her desire for Civakan and returns to him.
1601.nuance: Line 2 (விட்டா ளார்வ மவன்க ணிவன்மேன் மைந்துறவினான்) and மனைதுறந்தாள் in line 3 are hard to construe; the reading follows the sense that the episode needs, that her desire passes from Civakan back to the husband.

1602.reading: He bowed to the mountain like a tusker, with clouds falling on its brow like a painted cloth, streams of white waterfalls for its face-band, and gold flowing from it like rut, and climbed it holding to the bamboo's base.
1602.event: Civakan worships the mountain and climbs it.
1602.nuance: The mountain is described part by part as an elephant (மத்தகம், ஓடை, மதம், குஞ்சரம்), and the climber mounts it like a mahout. வேய்முதற் றூசங்கொண் is obscure.

1603.reading: On one side, as long-eyed women climbed the hill so that their accumulated evil deeds might leave them, their pale gold anklets rubbed and the whole ground there was red with lac, like lightning lying on darkness.
1603.event: Women climb the sacred hill to be rid of their sins.

claims.claim: climbing the holy hill removes the evil deeds one has piled up

1603.nuance: The hill is a shrine whose god is praised in 1608 onward as the ageless First One and the conqueror of Kama, which in this epic marks the Jina; the verse itself names no school, only the pilgrims' purpose.

1604.reading: On another side the crowd of people carrying sandal paste, garlands, cool fragrant powder, chosen incense and offerings, and holding up golden lamps, was so thick there was no room to stand.
1604.event: Crowds of worshippers carrying offerings throng the hill.
1604.nuance: The offerings listed (சாந்து, கோதை, சுண்ணம், புகை) are the same scents and garlands Civakan stripped from the body in 1583; here they are carried to the god.

links.note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews, skin, flesh and grease and asks which part is the garlanded woman; 1583 gives nearly the same list (குடர்கள், வழும்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்) but starts from the adorned hair and adds the three humours.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant catalogue is put in the mouth of a hero who is not renouncing, as a weapon against another man's wife, so the meditation on the foul body becomes a householder's defence against adultery rather than a step out of the world.

gains.a: a recognised ascetic form, the list of tissues, that tells the reader Civakan's reply is a teaching and not merely a rebuff
gains.b: a dramatic occasion: a particular woman pressing a particular man, against whom the list is used and proves effective

links.note: Siddhar 301 also strips the body to wind, bile and phlegm and foul matter, but the poet confesses he still runs after women and begs the Lord's grace to free him; Civakan recites the catalogue and simply refuses.
links.teaches: The same catalogue that the Saiva poet finds powerless without grace is, in the Jain epic, enough by itself to master desire, which shows the two traditions disagreeing about whether self-knowledge alone can free a man from lust.

gains.a: a contrast that brings out how self-reliant Civakan's restraint is: no god is asked for help
gains.b: a case where the catalogue works without grace, which makes the Siddhar's plea a claim about his tradition and not a fact about the body

links.note: Naladiyar 41 says that if skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from the body a stick is needed to drive off crows; 1584 opens the body and sets crows at the eyes.
links.teaches: Both poets end the lover's gaze with crows at the body, but the epic uses the image on the living woman standing before the hero, turning a general memento into a refusal spoken to her face.

gains.a: a traditional image whose force a Tamil reader already knows, which lets the hero's rebuff be brief
gains.b: evidence that the crow at the torn skin was a stock figure that a narrative poet could place in a scene

links.note: At 1577 Civakan reflects to himself that the body is a flesh-filled hut (ஊன்பயில் குரம்பை) of bone, sinew, blood and skin with nine gates; at 1584 he tells the woman it is a worm-filled hut (புழுப்பயில் குரம்பை).
links.teaches: The hut image moves from the hero's private thought when the woman first appears to his spoken answer to her, so the reader sees that his rebuff was prepared in silent meditation before she spoke.

links.note: At 1585 Civakan says the kavya poets have dressed up the flesh to kindle desire; at 1482, lying in Kemasari's house, he himself laments that her hair, brows, eyes and breasts kill him.
links.teaches: The hero who now condemns the poets' painting of the body was a few scenes before its most eloquent practitioner, so the epic sets its own love poetry under judgement and leaves the reader to weigh whether desire for a wife differs from desire for another's.

links.note: Naladiyar 44 refuses the petty men who call eyes water-lilies, carp and spears; 1585 blames the poets of kavya by name for painting brows, eyes and nose on a bag of skin.
links.teaches: Where the Naladiyar's opponents are anonymous fools, the epic names its own craft as the source of the illusion, so the critique of the simile becomes a self-critique of the epic genre.

gains.a: a precedent that makes Civakan's attack on poets part of an older ascetic argument rather than a passing jibe
gains.b: an identification of who the praisers of eyes are: the poets of the great poems, not only foolish lovers

links.note: At 1580 the woman tells Civakan that a Vidyadhara carried her off and his wife made him drop her in the forest; at 1592 her husband says she sent him for water and was gone when he came back.
links.teaches: The husband's plain account exposes the woman's story as a lie told to the hero, so the reader learns that her helpless plight was itself part of the seduction.

links.note: Pavadattan swears that after seeing him his wife never looked at another man; at 1581 she has begged Civakan to take her or let her die.
links.teaches: The husband's certainty about his wife's chastity is false in the reader's sight, and Civakan's silent laugh, not exposure, is how the epic lets the household survive the truth.

links.note: Kural 414 says listening to the learned is a support in one's faltering (ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை); 1595 says learning is a companion to the heart in its weakness (மெலிவிற்கோர் துணை) and asks the learned Pavadattan why he grieves.
links.teaches: The epic applies the Kural's promise to a man of many treatises and shows it failing: his learning does not console him, and he is comforted only when a mantra returns his wife.

gains.a: the authority of a Kural teaching, which makes Civakan's rebuke to the grieving scholar a reasoned one
gains.b: a test case in which the support learning offers is tried against the loss of a wife and found insufficient

links.note: Kural 57 says the guard of confinement is useless and the best guard is the one women's own நிறை keeps; 1597 says women do not hold their restraint within (உண்ணிறை யுடைய வல்ல) and yield to pressing.
links.teaches: The Kural trusts the guard inside a woman, the epic's hero denies most women have it, and the story of this chapter is offered as his proof, so the two texts disagree on whether a woman's restraint can be relied on at all.

gains.a: a precise contrary, the Kural's நிறை, that shows the hero's view as a position taken against a known teaching
gains.b: a narrative challenge to its trust, in which a wife thought steadfast is not

links.note: Kural 55 promises that the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; 1598 describes chaste wives who live worshipping their husband's hands (கணவற்கை தொழுது வாழ்வார்) as a few against the many of 1597.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's figure of the husband-worshipping wife but makes her a rare exception within women's general frailty, and drops the rain, so her power shrinks to ending her husband's distress.

gains.a: a known ideal against which the hero's two-part teaching on women can be measured
gains.b: a reading in which the husband-worshipping wife is defined by her renunciations in his absence, not by power over nature

links.note: Siddhar 910 calls the mountain of Ekambar the one that removes the hard deeds of those who bow (பணிவாரருவினை தீர்க்கும்); in 1603 women climb a hill so that their accumulated evil deeds may leave them (நிரைத்த தீவினை நீங்க).
links.teaches: A Jain epic and a Saiva poet share the belief that a sacred hill wears away karma, which shows a common practice of pilgrimage beneath the doctrinal quarrel over how deeds are destroyed.

gains.a: evidence that the pilgrims' purpose is a widely held Tamil belief and not a doctrine peculiar to the epic's hill
gains.b: a parallel from another faith that shows the hill's power over karma as shared ground rather than a Saiva claim alone

links.note: Siddhar 696 says the poet wandered over every forest and hill until his legs ached without seeing the Lord who moved within his body; 1603 shows crowds climbing a hill to shed their sins.
links.teaches: Within the Saiva tradition itself the climb that the epic describes approvingly is mocked as wasted walking, so the pairing shows the Siddhars turning against a practice that Jains and Saivas otherwise held in common.

gains.a: a critic's view that shows what the epic's narrator takes for granted in describing the pilgrims
gains.b: a picture of the very pilgrimage the Siddhar rejects, with its anklets, lac and crowds

source_issues: Most stanzas (all but 1586, 1596, 1602-1604) were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build; the joins look right.
1584 line 2 (பொல்லாத் தடிதடித் கீழ்ந்த போழ்தில்) looks corrupt; தடித் கீழ்ந்த is not a regular form.
1594 line 1 (என்ன பெயாபு ரென்றாற்கு) is evidently miswritten, perhaps for a form of பெயரீர்.
1596 line 4 பிறார்கண் and 1598 line 4 சோந்தவன் look like misprints (for பிறர்கண், சேர்ந்தவன்).
1601 line 2 (மைந்துறவினான்) and the construction of lines 2-3 are doubtful.
